labels.given: Given in a fictional scene, not externally verified observation
labels.interpretation: Interpretation or assumption, not established by the scene
labels.proposal: Proposed design, not a tested result
labels.evidence: What evidence would be needed in real use; none collected here

cases.title: The doorway that invites a story
cases.question: What can be described before a motive is assigned?
cases.setting: A fictional corridor at a shared learning centre. Someone approaches a doorway, pauses, glances to one side and walks back.
given: The person approached a doorway.
They paused, looked to one side and walked back.
No explanation from the person is included.
cases.unknown: Whether they changed plans, noticed a sign, heard a sound, or simply chose another route.

designA.name: V1 — Explain the behaviour
designA.action: Begin the discussion by asking participants why the person turned back.
designA.constraint: Questions about inner states can frame one guess as the answer.

designB.name: V2 — Separate observation and explanation
designB.action: Ask for one camera-checkable statement, two possible hypotheses and a missing-context question.
designB.constraint: Multiple hypotheses take time; the facilitator must not reward confident mind-reading.

cases.tradeoff: A careful discussion may move slower than a rapid explanation, but it can preserve uncertainty and reduce unjustified labels.
cases.review: Can a reviewer identify the observable statement without treating any proposed motive as a fact?
cases.evidence: Review the wording for clear observed/inferred separation; for a real learning session, gather optional feedback on clarity with appropriate consent.
cases.facilitation: “Tell me one action a camera could show, then one thing we cannot know yet.”

cases.title: A tote, a route, a purpose
cases.question: When we move the table, what else changes?
cases.setting: In a fictional shop, a tote sits on a counter and must be moved to a table. A chair and another visitor share the route.
given: The intended goal is to clear the counter.
The tote has two handles in the drawing.
The path includes a turn around a chair.
cases.interpretation: Moving the table closer will definitely make the task easier for everyone.
cases.unknown: Tote weight, individual preferences, passage widths, traffic, reach and whether the table blocks other users.

designA.name: V1 — Shorten the path
designA.action: Move the table next to the counter on the plan.
designA.constraint: The shorter route might reduce shared passage space.

designB.name: V2 — Design for both tasks and circulation
designB.action: Try a nearby table position while preserving a usable shared route; ask what real measurements are needed.
designB.constraint: A diagram cannot determine actual access or individual task suitability.

cases.tradeoff: Distance may improve while crowding or reach gets worse. One variable never explains the whole arrangement.
cases.review: What observable information would distinguish a shorter drawn route from a genuinely more usable task?
cases.evidence: Document actual dimensions and seek input from people who use the space before claiming improved access or effort.
cases.facilitation: “Name the goal first, then the objects, path, time and people. Which condition did we change?”

cases.title: Two paths to the reading room
cases.question: Why might a longer path offer a better choice?
cases.setting: A fictional library plan shows a direct route through a narrow doorway and a longer route through a shared corridor with unclear signage.
given: Route A is shorter in the sketch.
Route A has a visibly marked narrow doorway.
Route B takes more turns and passes an unclear sign.
cases.interpretation: The longer route is accessible, because it avoids the narrow door.
cases.unknown: Actual clear widths, slopes, door operation, surface, rest opportunities, sign visibility and the visitors' experience.

designA.name: V1 — Send everyone along Route B
designA.action: Place one arrow directing all visitors toward the longer corridor.
designA.constraint: The corridor signage and route conditions are not verified.

designB.name: V2 — Offer informed alternatives
designB.action: Clarify both options, remove temporary obstructions where feasible and verify real constraints before directing visitors.
designB.constraint: Improving information does not certify physical usability or building-code compliance.

cases.tradeoff: A clearer wayfinding system could add clutter; a shorter path could be constrained by its doorway.
cases.review: What would we need to measure, observe and ask before promoting either route?
cases.evidence: Conduct a genuine site survey and appropriately consented user review; check applicable local standards separately.
cases.facilitation: “Our sketch tells us about the drawing. What would we have to inspect in the building?”

cases.title: The rule that silenced a contribution
cases.question: Does less talking mean less participation?
cases.setting: Four fictional adults build a bridge from paper. A rule allows one builder to touch materials while others can only give spoken instructions.
given: One participant handles the paper.
Two participants speak during the task.
One participant draws and speaks very little.
cases.interpretation: The quiet participant has no ideas or is disengaged.
cases.unknown: Whether the participant chose a drawing route, found spoken turns useful, or wanted to contribute in another way.

designA.name: V1 — Keep speaking-only contributions
designA.action: Ask everyone except the builder to explain ideas out loud.
designA.constraint: The rule narrows valid contribution formats and can generate public pressure.

designB.name: V2 — Negotiate contribution modes
designB.action: Offer voluntary building, sketching, feedback and observation, with clear transitions between roles.
designB.constraint: More options can introduce material crowding or unclear group responsibilities.

cases.tradeoff: Expanded choice is promising on paper, but does not demonstrate actual belonging or quality of group participation.
cases.review: Does the invitation explicitly allow multiple meaningful modes without assigning individuals to them?
cases.evidence: Check the written roles, observe real use only with appropriate safeguards, and seek optional, privacy-respecting feedback.
cases.facilitation: “You can sketch, build, describe or observe. What does each contribution help the group discover?”

cases.title: One passing game, three cultures
cases.question: Can a scoreboard tell us who belongs?
cases.setting: Four fictional adults pass a ball in a park, during sports-club practice and in an adult learning group.
given: The same passing movement occurs in three story settings.
The club can count completed passes.
The learning group may change a rule to investigate it.
cases.interpretation: A higher pass count shows better inclusion or more enjoyment.
cases.unknown: Who felt invited, what participation formats were usable, and how participants interpreted the experience.

designA.name: V1 — Score only completed passes
designA.action: Use a pass count to describe success across all three settings.
designA.constraint: A metric about a defined action is not a metric of belonging or experience.

designB.name: V2 — Keep the count within its scope
designB.action: Describe the pass count, ask about roles and space, and add voluntary reflection without ranking individuals.
designB.constraint: More questions require respectful consent and may not produce a single comparable score.

cases.tradeoff: A simple number is easy to compare; an honest cultural account is richer but less reducible to a leaderboard.
cases.review: Which conclusion is supported by a count, and which requires other evidence?
cases.evidence: Define the scoring method and limits, then seek voluntary feedback if conducting a real programme evaluation.
cases.facilitation: “What did the score measure? What important question did it leave unanswered?”

cases.title: Five minutes, several invitations
cases.question: Does one instruction create the same opportunity for everyone?
cases.setting: A fictional educator is designing a five-minute movement-and-observation invitation in a room with close desks and different participation preferences.
given: The proposed window is five minutes.
Desks restrict shared space in the scenario.
The educator wants a predictable closing transition.
cases.interpretation: Any child who remains seated is not participating or needs a diagnosis.
cases.unknown: Room clearances, student preferences, specific support arrangements, school safeguards and suitability for any real group.

designA.name: V1 — A single required action
designA.action: Tell the group to stand and imitate the same movements.
designA.constraint: One required body position excludes alternatives and may draw attention to individuals.

designB.name: V2 — Voluntary routes toward one purpose
designB.action: Offer observation, seated or standing alternatives as appropriate, describe transitions, and close without ranking.
designB.constraint: Choice needs understandable directions, supervision and local adaptation; no health or attention benefit is established.

cases.tradeoff: A simple instruction takes less explanation; real choice can take more preparation and must remain genuinely optional.
cases.review: Can a teacher identify the task purpose, safe spatial limits, available alternatives and stop cue from the plan?
cases.evidence: Evaluate the written plan and local school/safeguarding requirements; do not collect child identities or claim cognitive effects.
cases.facilitation: “Which options fit the room? You can participate by describing, observing or choosing an appropriate movement.”

cases.title: A facilitator who listens to the room
cases.question: What should change after the first workshop design?
cases.setting: Six fictional adults join a 20-minute paper-bridge learning encounter with shared materials, some noise and different preferred ways to contribute.
given: The initial written script allows speaking-only contributions.
A fictional facilitator has 20 minutes.
The goal is to examine how rules change group participation options.
cases.interpretation: A confident facilitator's script guarantees a successful or inclusive workshop.
cases.unknown: How real participants would experience the session, whether choices were usable, and which outcomes could be supported by evidence.

designA.name: V1 — Lecture then activity
designA.action: Explain rules for most of the encounter and request spoken feedback from everyone.
designA.constraint: Long instructions and public speaking requirements can limit voluntary participation.

designB.name: V2 — Observe, name, design, facilitate, evaluate, improve
designB.action: Offer building, sketching or observing, plan transitions, separate evidence from interpretations and document one justified revision.
designB.constraint: The revised design remains untested; a neat rubric cannot certify real learning or inclusion.

cases.tradeoff: The improved script takes more planning but allows a clearer review of choices, boundaries and unanswered questions.
cases.review: Is the stated purpose supported by the invitation, timing, roles, privacy safeguards and a bounded evaluation question?
cases.evidence: Check the plan against predeclared criteria; only after appropriate consent and safeguards should real participants' optional feedback inform further change.
cases.facilitation: “Which part of the invitation should we improve—and what evidence makes that question worth asking?”
